Introduction
One of the central challenges in string theory is to determine whether it admits phe-nomenologically viable four-dimensional vacua. A realistic compactification should re-produce, at sufficiently low energies, the essential features of observed particle physics.A widely studied possibility is that the resulting four-dimensional theory contains an
N = 1 supersymmetric matter sector, with supersymmetry spontaneously broken atan energy scale compatible with phenomenological constraints. The properties of thefour-dimensional effective theory are determined by the vacuum configuration of thecompactification. In particular, quantities such as gauge couplings, Yukawa couplings,particle masses, and supersymmetry-breaking parameters depend on the vacuum ex-pectation values of scalar fields known as moduli. These fields parametrise continuousdeformations of the internal geometry, as well as other background data characterisingthe compactification.

For a long time, the presence of unstabilised moduli represented one of the mainobstacles to connecting string theory with low-energy phenomenology. Massless mod-uli would mediate long-range fifth forces and, since their vacuum expectation valuesenter directly into physical observables, would prevent the theory from making definitepredictions. Although perturbative and non-perturbative quantum effects are generi-cally expected to generate a potential for the moduli in four-dimensional N = 1 the-ories, a systematic and parametrically controlled mechanism for stabilising all of themremained unavailable for many years.

A major advance was provided by the development of flux compactifications and bythe systematic study of their role in moduli stabilisation [7–9]. Type IIB string compact-ifications provide a particularly suitable setting for this programme. In this framework,background three-form fluxes generate a superpotential for the axio-dilaton S and thecomplex-structure moduli za, allowing these fields to be stabilised at tree level. TheKähler moduli Tα, by contrast, remain unfixed at this order as a consequence of the no-scale structure of the tree-level effective theory. Their stabilisation therefore requireseffects that are absent at the classical level. In particular, the interplay between non-perturbative contributions to the superpotential [10] and perturbativeα′ corrections tothe Kähler potential [11,12] generates a non-trivial scalar potential for the Kähler sector.This potential can be analysed within a controlled expansion at large internal volumeand leads to the Large Volume Scenario [1], in which the overall volume of the compact-ification is stabilised at an exponentially large value. Such vacua provide a particularlyrich framework for studying supersymmetry breaking and its possible phenomenologi-
1



cal consequences.

The resulting hierarchy naturally suggests a two-step treatment of moduli stabili-sation. One first determines the supersymmetric tree-level vacuum of the axio-dilatonand complex-structure sector by imposing the supersymmetric condition, and subse-quently, treats the fields (S, za) as effectively frozen while analysing the subleadingdynamics responsible for the stabilisation of the Kähler moduli. This procedure cap-tures the leading structure of the vacuum and forms the basis of the conventional four-dimensional LVS effective theory. However, the separation between the two sectors isnot exact. The perturbative and non-perturbative effects responsible for Kähler-modulistabilisation depend, in general, on the axio-dilaton and complex-structure moduli. Oncethese contributions are included, the complete scalar potential develops non-vanishinggradients along the (S, za) directions. Consequently, the original tree-level flux vac-uum is displaced from its supersymmetric position [2,6]. The assumption that the flux-stabilised fields remain exactly frozen therefore neglects their backreaction on the fullvacuum.

The purpose of this thesis is to investigate this effect systematically. In particular, wedetermine explicitly the displacement of the axio-dilaton and complex-structure vac-uum induced by the subleading corrections responsible for Kähler-moduli stabilisation.The corrected minimum is computed perturbatively around the tree-level flux vacuum,organising the analysis according to the parametric dependence on the compactifica-tion volume V and the string coupling gs. Our results are derived in the controlledregime of exponentially large volume and weak string coupling,
V ≫ 1, gs ≪ 1. (0.1)

This allows us to identify the leading contributions to the vacuum shifts and to de-termine their scaling in the simultaneous large-volume and weak-coupling expansions.Once the corrected vacuum configuration has been determined, one can compute thecorrespondingF -terms, which provide the relevant order parameters for supersymme-try breaking in the four-dimensional effective theory.

A central result of this analysis is that the contribution induced by the displacementof the vacuum is not parametrically negligible. For the axio-dilaton, the shift-inducedcorrection enters at the same order in the simultaneous expansions in gs and V−1 asthe contribution obtained by evaluating the corrected F -terms at the unshifted tree-level vacuum. In the complex-structure direction, the effect is even more pronounced:
2



the shift-induced contribution is enhanced by an additional factor of g−1
s relative tothe corresponding unshifted term. Therefore, despite the smallness of the vacuum dis-placement itself, its effect on the F -terms can be of leading-order relevance, in theweak-coupling regime.We first study this mechanism in a simplified model with a rigid complex-structuresector, in which only the axio-dilaton S is displaced. We then extend the analysis toa model containing a dynamical complex-structure modulus and explicitly account forthe mixing between the S and z directions. This allows us to determine both the para-metric behaviour and the explicit form of the shifts δS and δz in the large-volume andweak-coupling expansions.

As previously stated, the corrections to the axio-dilaton and complex-structure F -terms can have direct phenomenological consequences. In sequestered LVS scenarios,soft supersymmetry-breaking terms depend sensitively on the auxiliary fields of theflux-stabilized sector [3]. We find that the shift of the vacuum does not parametricallymodify F S , so that soft terms whose leading contribution is controlled by the axio-dilaton auxiliary field retain the standard LVS scaling. By contrast, the modified complex-structure F -terms can give parametrically different contributions to observables whichdepend directly on F z, including scalar masses in the ultra-local regime.A further application concerns the supersymmetric partners of closed-string hiddenphotons. In type IIB orientifold compactifications, RR photons arise from the dimen-sional reduction of the RR four-form C(4) on orientifold-even three-cycles, and theirgauge kinetic functions are controlled by the complex-structure moduli [4, 13]. Con-sequently, the corresponding hidden-photino masses depend directly on the complex-structure F -terms. Therefore, any parametric modification of F za induced by the dis-placement of the flux vacuum is directly inherited by the hidden-photino mass, up tothe model-dependent complex-structure dependence of the gauge kinetic function.These examples provide a direct connection between the corrections studied in thiswork and the low-energy phenomenology of sequestered string compactifications.

This thesis is organised as follows. The first two chapters provide the theoreticalbackground required for the subsequent analysis. After reviewing the essential ele-ments of four-dimensional supergravity, we introduce the main features of superstringtheory and of Type IIB compactifications. Particular attention is devoted to the fieldcontent and effective description of Type IIB orientifolds with O3/O7-planes, with theaim of defining the quantities and conventions needed throughout the rest of the the-sis. Chapter 3 is devoted to the problem of moduli stabilisation. We first discuss the roleof background fluxes in fixing the axio-dilaton and complex-structure moduli and thenintroduce the Large Volume Scenario as a mechanism for stabilising the Kähler sector.

3



In this context, we emphasise the conventional two-step procedure in which the fluxsector is stabilised at tree level and subsequently treated as effectively frozen whenanalysing the subleading Kähler-moduli dynamics. The final chapter contains the orig-inal results of this work. We compute explicitly the displacement of the flux-stabilisedvacuum induced by the perturbative and non-perturbative corrections responsible forLVS stabilisation. The analysis is first carried out in a simplified toy model with rigidcomplex structure and is then extended to a more general setting including a dynamicalcomplex-structure modulus. We finally determine the corresponding corrections to theaxio-dilaton and complex-structure F -terms and analyse their parametric behaviour inthe large-volume and weak-coupling regime.

4



1 Supersymmetry and Supergravity
Supersymmetry is a spacetime symmetry relating bosonic and fermionic degrees offreedom and organizing them into common supermultiplets. It plays a fundamentalrole in superstring theory, whose development was historically motivated by the at-tempt to incorporate fermionic excitations into the bosonic string.The low-energy dynamics of string compactifications is naturally described in termsof supersymmetric field theories. In four-dimensional compactifications preserving foursupercharges, the relevant framework is N = 1 supersymmetry. We therefore beginthis chapter by reviewing the basic structure of four-dimensional rigid supersymmetry,introducing its algebra, the corresponding supermultiplets, and the supersymmetric ac-tions.We then turn to local supersymmetry, obtained by promoting the parameters of su-persymmetry transformations to spacetime-dependent spinors. Such a local symmetrycannot be consistently realized without introducing gravity: the corresponding gaugetheory necessarily contains the graviton, together with its fermionic superpartner, thegravitino. The resulting framework is N = 1, D = 4 supergravity.Finally, we present the supergravity action for chiral and vector multiplets coupledto gravity, emphasizing the role of the Kähler potential, the superpotential, and thegauge kinetic functions. Particular attention will be devoted to the scalar potential andto the auxiliary F -terms, which provide the essential language for describing modulistabilization and supersymmetry breaking in four-dimensional effective theories arisingfrom string compactifications.

1.1.2 The supersymmetry algebra

The Coleman–Mandula theorem [14] states that, under a set of physically reasonableassumptions, the most general symmetry algebra of a non-trivial interacting relativisticquantum field theory has to be a direct product of the Poincaré algebra with an internalsymmetry algebra. In particular, the theorem assumes that the full symmetry algebrais an ordinary Lie algebra, whose product is given only by commutators. This assump-tion can be relaxed by allowing also anticommutators between fermionic generators.The resulting structure is not an ordinary Lie algebra, but a Z2-graded Lie algebra, orLie superalgebra. 1.4 Supersymmetry breaking
If supersymmetry is realized in Nature, it cannot be an exact symmetry at the energyscales currently accessible to experiments. Indeed, exact supersymmetry would requirethe bosonic and fermionic states belonging to the same supermultiplet to have identicalmasses. No such mass degeneracy has been observed in the spectrum of elementaryparticles.Supersymmetry must therefore be broken at some characteristic scale, which wedenote by MSUSY. At energies much larger than this scale, the effects responsiblefor the breaking may become negligible, and the theory approaches its supersymmet-ric limit. This statement is particularly natural when supersymmetry is broken by softterms.There are two conceptually distinct ways in which supersymmetry may be broken:

• Spontaneous supersymmetry breaking. The Lagrangian is exactly supersymmet-ric, but the vacuum is not invariant under the action of the supercharges. In aglobally supersymmetric theory, this occurs when at least one auxiliary field ac-quires a non-vanishing vacuum expectation value.
• Explicit supersymmetry breaking. The Lagrangian contains terms which are not in-variant under supersymmetry transformations. A generic explicit breaking wouldspoil the ultraviolet cancellations which motivate supersymmetry. One thereforeusually restricts to soft supersymmetry-breaking terms, which do not reintroducequadratic ultraviolet divergences. Their coefficients have positive mass dimen-sion, so their effects become progressively less important at energies much largerthan the supersymmetry-breaking scale.
Typical soft-breaking operators include scalar mass terms, gaugino masses and scalartrilinear and bilinear interactions. Although these terms explicitly break supersymme-try, they preserve the improved ultraviolet behaviour of the supersymmetric theory.

2 Superstrings
In this chapter, we review the main ingredients of type II superstring theory that arerequired for the compactification framework developed in the remainder of this thesis[15]. We begin with the Ramond–Neveu–Schwarz formulation of superstrings in ten-dimensional flat Minkowski spacetime, emphasizing the role of worldsheet fermions,the Neveu–Schwarz and Ramond sectors, and the GSO projection. The latter removesthe tachyonic state and leads to a spectrum containing both spacetime bosons andfermions, organized into supersymmetric multiplets.Among the five consistent superstring theories in ten dimensions, type IIA, type IIB,type I, and the two heterotic theories with gauge groups SO(32) and E8 × E8, wefocus on the type II theories, and in particular on type IIB string theory, which providesthe ten-dimensional starting point for the compactifications considered in this work.We therefore review it massless spectra and its corresponding low-energy supergravitydescriptions.We then turn to compactifications on Calabi–Yau threefolds. After introducing thegeometric and cohomological properties of Calabi–Yau manifolds, we discuss how theten-dimensional massless fields give rise to four-dimensional fields through Kaluza–Klein reduction. Compactification of type II string theory on a Calabi–Yau threefold pre-servesN = 2 supersymmetry in four dimensions. To obtain theN = 1 effective theoryrelevant for moduli stabilization, we subsequently introduce orientifold projections andspecialize to type IIB Calabi–Yau orientifolds withO3/O7-planes. This construction de-termines the surviving moduli fields and their organization into four-dimensional chiraland vector multiplets, providing the setting in which fluxes, the effective Kähler poten-tial, and the corrections to the moduli F -terms will be studied.

2.4 Type II orientifolds
Orientifold projections of Type II Calabi–Yau compactifications provide a standard mech-anism for reducing four-dimensional supersymmetry from N = 2 to N = 1. They in-troduce orientifold planes and require the inclusion of D-branes for Ramond–Ramondcharge cancellation, thereby also giving rise to gauge sectors and charged matter in thefour-dimensional effective theory.Starting from Type II string theory compactified on a Calabi–Yau threefold X3, onequotients the theory by a discrete orientifold action involving worldsheet parity and aninvolution of the internal manifold. Depending on the Type II theory and on the classof orientifold, the orientifold operator takes the form

O = (−1)FLΩσ. (2.83)
Here Ω reverses the orientation of the string worldsheet, FL is the spacetime fermionnumber in the left-moving sector, and σ is an involutive isometry of the internal Calabi–Yau manifold,

σ2 = id. (2.84)
The precise form of O, as well as the action of σ on the Calabi–Yau geometry, dependson the orientifold construction under consideration.The geometric fixed loci of σ support orientifold planes. An Op-plane extends alongthe four non-compact spacetime dimensions and wraps an internal cycle of real dimen-sion p−3. In the standard orientifold constructions considered here, these objects carrynegative Ramond–Ramond charge and negative tension. Their total Ramond–Ramondcharge must be cancelled by appropriate configurations of D-branes and, when rele-vant, background fluxes. This requirement is encoded in the corresponding Ramond–Ramond tadpole-cancellation conditions.Spacetime-filling D-branes extend along the four non-compact dimensions and wrapinternal cycles of X3. They need not wrap the same cycles as the orientifold planes.Rather, the total charge carried by the D-branes and their orientifold images must can-cel the charges of the orientifold planes, together with any flux-induced contributions,in the appropriate homology or cohomology class. Open strings ending on the D-branesgive rise to four-dimensional gauge fields and charged matter multiplets.Preservation of four-dimensional N = 1 supersymmetry imposes further condi-tions on the involution σ. In Type IIB orientifolds, σ acts holomorphically on the Calabi–Yau manifold, whereas in the standard Type IIA constructions it acts antiholomorphi-cally. Its action assigns definite parities to the Kähler form J , the holomorphic three-form Ω, and the ten-dimensional form fields. The orientifold projection retains onlythe degrees of freedom invariant under the combined action O, thereby truncating theoriginal four-dimensional N = 2 spectrum to an N = 1 spectrum.

3 Large Volume Scenario
The four-dimensional massless spectrum arising from string compactifications gener-ally contains a large number of scalar fields, known as moduli. In Type IIB Calabi–Yauorientifold compactifications with O3/O7-planes, whose field content is summarized inTable 2, these fields parametrise continuous deformations of the internal geometry anddetermine several effective four-dimensional couplings. If they remain unstabilized, themoduli correspond to flat directions of the scalar potential and may give rise to lightscalar degrees of freedom. Such fields can mediate long-range interactions and inducephenomenological effects that are incompatible with current observations. A realisticstring compactification must therefore provide a mechanism that lifts these flat direc-tions, fixes the vacuum expectation values of the moduli, and generates sufficientlylarge masses for them.In this chapter, we review the Large Volume Scenario (LVS), which provides a sys-tematic framework for moduli stabilization in Type IIB flux compactifications. The sta-bilization mechanism proceeds hierarchically. At leading order, background three-formfluxes stabilize the axio-dilaton and the complex-structure moduli at a supersymmetricminimum, while the Kähler moduli remain unfixed as a consequence of the no-scalestructure. Their stabilization is subsequently achieved by including perturbative α′ cor-rections to the Kähler potential together with non-perturbative contributions to the su-perpotential. This two-step structure will play a central role in the analysis developedin the remainder of this thesis.

58

4 Corrections to the F-terms
In Large Volume Scenarios, the F -terms F S and F za receive non-vanishing contribu-tions from several subleading effects, some of which have already been extensivelystudied in the literature [1–5]. For instance, the inverse of the corrected Kähler met-ric, K0 + δK, induces mixing between the (S, za) sector and the Ti directions. Since
DTi

W is non-zero at the LVS AdS minimum, this mixing generates non-vanishing F -terms for both S and za. In addition, the correction δK directly modifies the covariantderivatives DTi
, DS , and Dza . The dependence of Wnp on za and S via its prefactor:

−aiT

i also leads the F -terms to acquire non-zero contributions.In this work, a different source of correction is addressed: the displacement of theexpectation values of S and za away from their leading-order vacuum (3.33). Moreprecisely, how the shift δS and δz feeds into the F -terms is here studied.Usually the dilaton is stabilized at leading order by background fluxes (3.1), however,perturbative and non-perturbative effects can shift it away from its original minimum.In this final chapter, we implement the mechanism described above explicitly. Afterreviewing the corrections to the moduli F -terms previously discussed in the literature,we identify and estimate the additional contributions induced by the displacement ofthe flux-stabilized fields from their tree-level supersymmetric values.We first analyse the effect perturbatively in a simplified Large Volume Scenariomodel, keeping track of both the inverse-volume and weak-coupling expansions. Thetoy model is chosen to have a rigid complex-structure sector, h2,1 = 0, together with theminimal number of Kähler moduli required to realise an LVS vacuum, namely h1,1 = 2.This setting allows us to isolate the shift of the axio-dilaton and to determine its contri-bution to the corresponding auxiliary field F S .The most significant result emerges when the analysis is extended to a model con-taining one complex-structure modulus z, corresponding to h2,1 = 1. In this setting, thesubleading effects responsible for LVS stabilisation displace both the axio-dilaton andthe complex-structure modulus from their supersymmetric flux vacuum. We find thatthe resulting shift-induced contribution to F z is parametrically enhanced in the weak-coupling regime. More precisely, within the perturbative expansion and assumptionsadopted here, this contribution carries one additional inverse power of gs relative tothe standard estimate reported in Ref. [3].For the axio-dilaton F -term, by contrast, the contribution generated by the dis-placement of S is generically of the same parametric order as the corrections previ-ously identified in Ref. [2]. It therefore competes with the standard LVS contributionat the same order in both the inverse-volume and weak-coupling expansions. 5 Conclusions and Outlook
The Large Volume Scenario is commonly analysed through a two-step procedure. Attree level, background fluxes stabilise the axio-dilaton and the complex-structure mod-uli at a supersymmetric vacuum, while the Kähler moduli remain unfixed because ofthe no-scale structure. Perturbative and non-perturbative effects are then included tostabilise the Kähler sector, treating the flux-stabilised fields as effectively frozen at theirtree-level values.This separation provides a controlled description of the vacuum at leading orderin the inverse-volume expansion. It is, however, not exact. The effects responsible forKähler-moduli stabilisation depend in general on the axio-dilaton and complex-structuremoduli and therefore generate non-vanishing gradients along these directions. As aconsequence, the tree-level flux vacuum is displaced once the complete scalar poten-tial is taken into account.The purpose of this thesis has been to study this displacement systematically andto determine how it modifies the auxiliary fields associated with the flux-stabilised sec-tor. Particular attention has been devoted to the simultaneous large-volume and weak-coupling expansions,

V ≫ 1, gs ≪ 1, (5.1)
which provide the parametric control required by the four-dimensional effective de-scription.The corrected vacuum was determined perturbatively by separating the scalar po-tential into its leading flux contribution and the subleading terms. This procedure makesexplicit that the magnitude of the displacement is determined not only by the correct-ing potential, but also by the inverse Hessian of the tree-level flux vacuum. Analysis of the harmonic flow

of geometric structures

Eric Loubeau
Département de Mathématiques
LMBA / UMR 6205
Université de Bretagne Occidentale
6, avenue Victor Le Gorgeu
CS 93837, 29238 Brest Cedex 3, France
eric.loubeau@univ-brest.fr

Received: March 5, 2025; accepted: June 10, 2025.

Abstract. We develop an analysis of the flow of harmonic H-structures with the strategy
introduced by Chen-Struwe for the harmonic map heat equation when the target does not
necessarily have negative sectional curvature, so the Eells-Sampson Theorem cannot apply.

In particular, this flow method enables us to find theoretical hypotheses under which the
existence of a torsion-free H-structure is guaranteed and conditions for which the flow must
blow up in finite time.

This extends results already known for some specific groups like U(n), G2 or Spin(7).

Keywords: Geometric structures; harmonic maps; harmonic sections, heat flow

MSC 2020 classification: primary 53C10, 53C15, 53C43, 58E20, 53E30

1 Holonomy and geometric structures

Berger’s 1955 theorem gives the list of the seven possible holonomy groups
of an irreducible, non-symmetric, simply-connected Riemannian n-dimensional
manifold: SO(n) (the general case), U(n2 ) (Kähler), SU(n2 ) (Calabi-Yau), Sp(n4 )
(Hyper-Kähler), Sp(n4 )Sp(1) (Quaternionic-Kähler), G2 (n = 7), Spin(7) (n =
8); plus the group Spin(9) for n = 16, before it was removed by Alekseevskij [1].

Moreover, each case is characterised by the existence of a parallel (multi-)
tensor, with respect to the Levi-Civita connection of (M, g).

For SO(n), it is the unobstructed condition of a torsion-free connection,
the Kähler case is equivalent to the existence of a parallel almost Hermitian
structure, etc.

For G2, the parallel three-form ϕ must, point-wise, be given in some frame
of TpM by

ϕp = e123 − e1 ∧ (e45 − e67) + e2 ∧ (e46 − e57) + e3 ∧ (e47 − e56),

while for Spin(7), Φ ∈ Λ4(T ∗M) and the local model is

Φp = e0123 − e0145 − e0167 − e0246 + e0257 − e0347 − e0356

+ e4567 − e2367 − e2345 − e1357 + e1346 − e1256 − e1247

where

e0123 = dx0 ∧ dx1 ∧ dx2 ∧ dx3.

The significance of holonomy is twofold. First, it informs on the curvature tensor
as it must live in the holonomy Lie algebra and this implies for SU(n2 ), Sp(n4 ),
G2 and Spin(7) that the manifold is Ricci-flat.

On the other hand, manifolds with special holonomy are the cornerstone
of higher-dimensional Gauge Theory. For example, take n = 7 and G2, then
a vector bundle E → M7 with connection ∇ has curvature F∇ ∈ Λ2, so the
condition ∗F∇ = λF∇ (λ ∈ R) does not make sense anymore and we must
introduce a three-form to counterbalance the degrees. If chosen closed, it will
allow for Yang-Mills connections.

The disadvantage is that it is generally hard to construct manifolds with spe-
cial holonomy, as the problem is highly non-linear, especially when the defining
tensor determines the metric. For example, local solutions of G2-manifolds first
appear in 1984 [3], complete ones in 1986 [4] and compact constructions only as
late as 1996-2000 with Joyce [15, 16].

An alternative, softer and more topological in nature, is to consider H-
structures (H ⊂ SO(n)), which are reductions of the structure group and can
also be seen as sections of an ad-hoc twistor space constructed as the H-quotient
of the unitary frame bundle PSO(n).

Locally, H-structures are described by (multi-) tensors given at each point
by a Euclidean prototype and stabilized by the group H.

It relies on a model (p, q)-tensor ξ0 ∈ T p,q(Rn) on the Euclidean space,
stabilised by the group H = Stab(ξ0) = {g ∈ GL(n,R) : g.ξ0 = ξ0} under the
GL(n,R) right action

g.ξ0 = ξ

In fact, this approach goes further than Berger’s list and includes new cases

(i.e. global orthonormal frames for H = {1}) or unit vector fields (H = SO(n−

Finally, one should add that H-structures with torsion, i.e. non-parallel, are
key ingredients in several theories of Mathematical Physics, for example the

and Tsimpis [19]. This fact alone should be sufficient reason for their study.

2 Harmonic maps and harmonicity

For an abstract (smooth) map φ from a compact Riemannian manifold
(M, g) to (N,h), the Dirichlet energy is

called harmonic maps [10] and the corresponding Euler-Lagrange equation is
the vanishing of the tension field

τ(φ) = trace∇dφ.

The energy functional is conformally invariant when dimM = 2 and harmonic
maps generalise harmonic functions (N = R), geodesics (dimM = 1), totally
geodesic maps (since ∇dφ = 0), minimal submanifolds (isometric immersions)
and holomorphic maps between Kähler manifolds. Cf. [2, Chap. 3] for details
and examples.

The groundbreaking work of Eells and Sampson [10] did not just introduced
this notion but also proved the existence of a harmonic representative in each
homotopy class when the target has non-positive sectional curvature. One should
however keep in mind that if there only exists a single homotopy class, it will
contain the trivially-harmonic constant maps.

Perhaps, as important was the heat-flow method they employed which has
known a rich legacy, all the way to Hamilton’s Ricci flow and Perelman’s proof
of the Poincaré conjecture.

This method is perhaps just as compelling by its failure when the curvature
condition on the target is not met and the flow develops bubbles and explodes,
as is the case of the sphere S2 to itself. This was superbly exploited by Sachs
and Uhlenbeck with a reparametrization process enabling to restart the flow
and accounting for the topological penalties in terms of energy quantization.

Paradoxically, for the two-sphere, these pitfalls of the heat flow can eas-
ily be circumvented by considering holomorphic maps and produce harmonic
representatives in each and every homotopy class.

The best-known situation where harmonic maps do not exist is for degree-
one maps from the two-torus to the two-sphere [11]. Indeed, such a map would



132 E. Loubeau

have to be conformal, hence holomorphic, which is forbidden for degree one by
Riemann-Roch.

In higher dimensions, one of the most often encountered example is the Hopf
map from S3 to S2 and, as a Riemannian submersion with minimal fibres, it also
happens to be a harmonic morphism.

In spite of decades of work on harmonic maps, relatively little has been done
for sections, except perhaps for vector fields [7], and C. M. Wood was the first to
consider almost Hermitian structures as sections of the twistor space and study
them under the light of harmonicity [20].

The point here is not merely to compute the tension field of a particular
map but more precisely to consider the Dirichlet energy of sections and search
for its critical points among sections, in order to compare like with like.

On a philosophical level, there is no reason to limit this to the specific case
of almost Hermitian structures and any type of reduction of structures on a
Riemannian manifold can be the subjected to the same treatment.

3 The Heat flow

The ultimate objective of the heat flow of geometric structures is to pro-
vide conditions ensuring the existence of an absolute minimiser of the Dirichlet
energy and answer the question of torsion-free geometric structures in a given
homotopy class.

With a target of positive curvature, one cannot hope to apply Eells-Sampson’s
original proof and must turn to Chen-Struwe’s arguments. In the end, this ap-
proach leads to a threshold for the Dirichlet energy of the initial data under
which convergence will happen to a torsion-free solution. By contraposition,
this lower bound can also be used to obtain singularity results.

This method is based on a series of more or less technical results but first,
one should recall that short-time existence is an automatic consequence of the
harmonic map equation. The main equation we will work with is the Bochner
formula which essentially turns the heat flow equation, living in the pull-back
of the vertical space of the twistor space, i.e. the bundle associated with the
isotropic representation, into a scalar expression at the cost of becoming an
inequality.

The Shi-type estimates control, along the flow, the norms of the derivatives
of the torsion (basically the coderivatives of the geometric structure) in terms
of the torsion itself and the derivatives of the curvature.

Both these results are valid for a general group H ⊂ SO(n) (and even more
cf. [9]).

The cornerstone of the whole strategy is the Almost Monotonicity Formula
(AMF) for a time-dependent functional which integrates, over a geodesic ball,
the product of the energy density and the backward heat kernel with singularity
at the centre of the ball (along with localisation by a cut-off function).



138 E. Loubeau

This AMF will prompt the ε-regularity of the heat flow which draws a point-
wise bound of the energy density from a bound on the integral of the function
involved in the AMF.

This opens the gates, not only for energy gap results but also for long-time
existence and finite-time singularity statements.

Indeed, by a refined treatment of the Bochner formula, due to Chen-Ding
[5], controlling the existence interval of the harmonic flow, one can prove that
if the energy density remains bounded over the maximal existence interval then
the flow exists for all time and converges to a harmonic solution.

On the other hand, if it explodes then the maximal existence-time must be
less than (the square-root of) the initial energy.

To conclude, bounds on the Dirichlet energy and L∞-norm of the initial data
exclude explosion of the energy density over the maximal existence interval,
hence force long-time existence and convergence toward a torsion-free solution.

Additionally, if no torsion-free H-structure exists in a given homotopy class
while the infimum of the Dirichlet energy is indeed zero, small enough initial
Dirichlet energy will make the flow develop a finite-time singularity.

Versions of these results for specific groups H can be found in [14, 8] but
note that groups like SU(n) are not covered by these results.

Assume (Mn, g) to be an oriented Riemannian n-manifold of bounded geom-
etry. In §1 we saw that a compatible H-structure ξ on (Mn, g) corresponds to a
section σ of π : Fr(M, g)/H →M . Now, there is a natural isomorphism between
π : Fr(M, g)/H → M and the associated bundle Fr(M, g) ×SO(n) SO(n)/H,
which, fibrewise, is an isometry with respect to the bi-invariant metric on SO(n).
The induced one-to-one correspondence between sections σ ∈ Γ(Fr(M, g)/H)
and SO(n)-equivariant maps s : Fr(M, g)→ SO(n)/H identifies solutions to the
harmonic section flow with SO(n)-equivariant solutions to the classical harmonic
map heat flow for maps Fr(M, g)→ SO(n)/H, where the target space SO(n)/H
is considered with its normal homogeneous Riemannian manifold structure.

As the short-time existence of the heat flow of harmonic maps is a stan-
dard consequence of the ellipticity of the tension field and the harmonic H-
flow is merely the vertical part of the heat flow for harmonic maps from M to
Fr(M)/H, its short-time existence is assured.

abstracts.value: Recently, influence of strong fields on nuclear decay processes is progressively becoming a topic of great interest plus the existence of some ambiguities. In this study, an approximate calculation of the Schrödinger equation with reduced <math><mi>r</mi></math> dependence is employed instead of the classical Coulomb wave-function program to provide a description of decay width and decay energy in quasistatic (adiabatic) laser fields. More importantly, going beyond the quasistatic approximation, the strict time evolution of the wave function and the periodic modulation of the decay energy are investigated by solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation with the split operator method, which captures the dynamical behavior of the <math><mi>α</mi></math> cluster during the decay process. First, our results corroborate earlier reports that the decay width is modified only negligibly by strong laser fields. Likewise, the shift in decay energy is found to be extremely small, which validates the rationality of using fixed experimental decay energies in earlier studies. This modification effect will exist more obviously in a nucleus with the higher proton-neutron asymmetry, the lower decay energy, and the octupole deformation. Second, our results demonstrate that strong fields can indeed produce a periodic modulation of decay energy, with a cycle mean shift on the order of <math><mrow><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup><mspace width="4pt"/><mi>eV</mi></mrow></math> at an intensity of <math><mrow><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>24</mn></msup><mspace width="4pt"/><mi mathvariant="normal">W</mi><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>cm</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>.

titles.title: Time evolution of the <math><mi>α</mi></math>-decay process in intense laser fields

abstracts.value: Spin squeezing is a genuine multipartite entanglement resource enabling quantum-enhanced metrology beyond classical limits. Based on a hybrid solid-state system of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers and magnons, we propose a scheme for generating spin squeezing via Kerr nonlinearity. In the large-detuning regime, by tuning the strength of the magnon parametric amplification (MPA) enabled by Kerr effect, the magnon-mediated spin-spin interactions can be controlled, thereby allowing flexible switching among one-axis twisting (OAT), two-axis twisting (TAT), and unconventional two-axis twisting (UTAT). Remarkably, in the presence of realistic dissipation and finite-size effects, an optimized UTAT interaction exhibits enhanced spin squeezing and quantum-enhanced sensing performance compared with the corresponding OAT and TAT cases. Furthermore, in the resonant and strongly dissipative regime, the MPA-induced TAT interaction and squeezed magnon reservoir jointly enable steady-state spin squeezing of the NV ensemble. Our results establish a unified and flexible scheme for generating both dynamical and steady-state spin squeezing, with potential applications in quantum-enhanced precision measurements.

titles.title: Dynamical and stable spin squeezing via magnon Kerr nonlinearity in a hybrid solid-state system

abstracts.value: We design an atom-waveguide system to achieve nonreciprocal frequency conversion. Single-photon frequency conversion is achieved through inelastic scattering mediated by the V-type giant atom with one transition coupled to a one-dimensional coupled-resonator waveguide (CRW) and the other transition coherently driven by a classical field. To quantitatively characterize the frequency-conversion efficiency, we define scattering flows by incorporating the corresponding group velocities. The reciprocity and nonreciprocity of the system can be characterized by the conversion-flow contrast. It is found that the single-photon frequency-conversion flow is closely related to the size of the giant atom and the phase difference between the coupling strengths at the two atom-CRW coupling sites. Under reciprocal conditions, the maximum conversion flow is strictly bounded by <math><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, regardless of how the giant atom size and the phase difference are tuned. When reciprocity is broken, tuning the coupling phase at a fixed giant atom size significantly enhances the maximum conversion flow, which can even reach unity. Meanwhile, the conversion-flow contrast reaches its extremal values, corresponding to perfect single-photon nonreciprocity.

titles.title: Nonreciprocal frequency conversion of single photons in a one-dimensional coupled-resonator waveguide

abstracts.value: In this note, I describe a quantum algorithm that prepares an arbitrary state $|ψ\rangle$ to inverse exponential precision in polynomial time by making queries to an $\mathsf{NP}$ oracle, assuming one can directly query entries of the state vector corresponding to $|ψ\rangle$. The previous best upper bound on the complexity class required by an oracle for this task was $\mathsf{PP}$. I provide evidence that $\mathsf{NP}$ is the best possible upper bound by showing that any quantum algorithm using a $\mathsf{P}$ oracle, or even a $\mathsf{P/poly}$ oracle, requires exponentially many queries. I also discuss some implications of this result for the $\mathsf{QMA}$ search-to-decision problem and unitary synthesis.

titles.title: State Synthesis with an NP oracle

abstracts.value: Quantum programs that use temporary values, known as \emph{ancilla} qubits, must explicitly \emph{uncompute} each ancilla back to zero to ensure that the program produces correct outputs. Conventional uncomputation uses unitary quantum gates, whereas leading quantum algorithms now leverage \emph{measurement-based uncomputation} (MBU), which replaces costly unitary $T$ gates with cheaper measurements and phase corrections. Current quantum programming frameworks can use measurement to uncompute specific gates such as Toffoli. No automatic transformation, however, accepts an arbitrary circuit whose ancillas are computed and uncomputed via the standard approach and converts the circuit to use MBU\@. Researchers instead apply MBU to individual circuit designs by hand, which limits algorithm development and compiler optimization. Such a transformation has not existed due to two fundamental unknowns: where MBU applies and which gates realize MBU for an arbitrary computation. To solve these, we first present a static analysis that identifies, for each ancilla qubit, each circuit position where measurement is sound --- subsuming basic assumptions that MBU only applies at the end of a circuit. Next, we present circuit transformations that soundly turn unitary uncomputation gates into efficient phase corrections after measurement --- generalizing rewrite rules from prior literature that are either limited to a single gate or not applicable to a general circuit. We present \textsf{MBUndo}, an integrated compiler pass that automatically converts circuits to measurement-based uncomputation. It requires no user annotations other than which qubits are ancillas, the same as needed by existing uncomputation synthesizers, and can enhance their output circuits. We evaluate \textsf{MBUndo} on 22 benchmarks to reveal \emph{T} gate reductions of ${>}36.5\%$ over uncomputation synthesizers.

titles.title: MBUndo: Sound, Automatic, and Efficient Measurement-Based Uncomputation for Quantum Circuits

abstracts.value: Quantum channel relative entropy can be nonadditive, making its regularization essential for asymptotic analysis. We study when the regularized value is attained at finite blocklength and how efficiently it can be approximated. For the first question, we establish a sharp dichotomy: the regularized value is either attained already at the single-copy level, implying additivity at every blocklength, or is never attained at any finite blocklength. Notably, a simple two-copy additivity test distinguishes between these alternatives for qubit channels and for channel pairs in arbitrary dimensions admitting an interior optimizer. We further show that both the interiority condition and finite nonattainment are generic, holding for almost every channel pair. For the second question, we establish explicit convergence rates for approximating the regularized channel relative entropy. For fixed channel dimensions, $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3/2})$ channel copies suffice to approximate the regularized value to additive accuracy $\varepsilon$. Alternatively, a semidefinite hierarchy achieves the same accuracy at level $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-2})$, yielding a certified polynomial-time approximation. Together, these results reveal the intriguing structure and generic behavior of regularized channel relative entropy, sharpening our understanding of both its analytical and computational aspects.

titles.title: Finite attainment and efficient computation of regularized quantum channel relative entropy

abstracts.value: Capacity-approaching quantum error correction faces a fundamental tension: the required parity-check matrices need to become increasingly dense, while practical decoding and syndrome extraction favor sparse, bounded-degree structures. Reconciling these competing requirements remains an important open problem in quantum code design. We construct Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code ensembles that approach the CSS rate over memoryless Pauli channels under maximum-likelihood decoding while retaining sparse, bounded-degree graphical representations. The construction separates parity-check density from graphical complexity: although capacity-approaching components may require dense parity-check matrices, they are represented by sparse concatenated factor graphs. We first study a construction combining low-density parity-check (LDPC) and low-density generator-matrix (LDGM) component codes and numerically analyze the average weight distributions of the resulting codes. Motivated by these results, we introduce a second construction based on concatenated LDPC and LDGM codes and generalized irregular repeat-accumulate (GIRA) codes. We derive bounds on the average weight distribution of the resulting sum ensemble and use the Miller-Burshtein framework to prove simultaneous reliability of the two CSS decoding components. Consequently, the proposed ensemble achieves rates arbitrarily close to the CSS hashing bound under separate bit- and phase-error correction, while maintaining bounded graphical complexity, thus providing a foundation for future iterative decoders and indirect syndrome-extraction architectures.

titles.title: Achievability of CSS codes performance limits over Pauli channels under separate ML decoding with bounded graphical complexity

abstracts.value: Simulation-trained generative models are emerging as a powerful framework for field-level inference in cosmology, particularly in strongly nonlinear regimes where analytical approaches become intractable. However, the finite size of training datasets often leads to variance shrinkage, indicating that part of the realization-level variability of the underlying physical process is not captured by the learned generative dynamics. In this Letter, we interpret variance shrinkage as a diagnostic of missing effective degrees of freedom and introduce physics-informed latent modifications to the generative dynamics of a continuous normalizing flow. We show that these latent corrections recover a substantial fraction of the missing variability without requiring additional training simulations. Using weak-lensing field-level inference as a representative cosmological application, we further demonstrate through posterior analysis that the learned latent directions are actively exploited during inference and behave as effective nuisance parameters that absorb part of the mismatch between the training and target distributions. As a result, the model exhibits improved robustness to out-of-distribution shifts in field-level inference. Our work establishes variance shrinkage as a practical diagnostic for identifying missing degrees of freedom in simulation-trained generative models and provides a framework for recovering them through physics-informed modifications of generative dynamics.

titles.title: Recovering Missing Degrees of Freedom in Simulation-Trained Field-Level Generative Models

abstracts.value: AI scientists are expanding automated research across scientific domains, yet their ability to turn the scientific record into a foundation for autonomous discovery remains elusive. Here we uncover a fundamental barrier to this transition and demonstrate a route to overcome it in computational quantum science, where advances shape both what we can learn from complex quantum systems and what quantum computing can ultimately deliver. To identify this barrier, we introduce OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment that converts published studies into executable reproduction tasks. Across 59 papers spanning classical simulation, quantum algorithms and quantum-property characterization, we systematically evaluate five agentic systems powered by large language models and six third-party agent harnesses. Our findings reveal that current AI scientists often fail to reproduce published results, exposing a fundamental mismatch between what scientific papers communicate and what autonomous agents require. By contrast, human expert intervention can turn these failures into successful reproductions, showing that the missing information can be identified and converted into reusable research experience. Guided by this observation, we develop Residual Agents (RA), a quantum-tailored self-improving AI scientist that distils externally verified workflow repairs into such experience. RA substantially improves research performance under fixed base models and limited adaptation budgets. For example, RA raises DeepSeek V4.1 Flash performance from 68% to 85%, matching Claude Code with Opus 5 at a third of its cost despite using a weaker base model. We integrate all reproduced results into an extensible platform built on the model context protocol, making verified research workflows directly accessible to AI scientists and allowing new scientific papers to be continuously incorporated.

titles.title: Reimagining computational quantum research with AI scientists

abstracts.value: We construct explicit two-sided lossless expanders whose binary adjacency matrices have full rank, and use them to obtain explicit asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes whose specified X- and Z-check matrices have full row rank and satisfy small-set soundness, or confinement, on a linear range. Our lossless expanders are a variant of those of Hsieh, Lubotzky, Mohanty, Reiner, and Zhang, with a free action of a finite 2-group. Under such an action, injectivity and surjectivity of the adjacency matrix are detected on a fixed-size matrix indexed by vertex orbits. Adding a sparse factor to the gadget at the middle vertices of a single type then enforces full rank, with a controlled loss in expansion. To obtain the 2-group action, we observe that reducing the generators of the Lubotzky-Phillips-Sarnak Ramanujan graphs modulo powers of 2, instead of modulo an odd prime, gives Ramanujan Cayley graphs on finite 2-groups. This construction may be of independent interest. Plugging two such expanders into the balanced product of Lin and Hsieh gives the quantum codes, since full rank of the input graphs is inherited by the check matrices. Our construction supplies the code family sought by Hong, Guo, and Lucas. Applying their analysis, within their framework and under their dynamical assumptions, gives quantum memories whose free-energy density is analytic at every positive temperature and whose guaranteed lifetime is $exp(Ω(N))$ at sufficiently low fixed positive temperature, where N is the blocklength. This improves the previously guaranteed stretched-exponential timescale.

titles.title: Full-Rank Constructions of Explicit Lossless Expanders and Good Small-Set qLTCs

abstracts.value: In quantum error correction, the decoder must estimate the errors from the measurement data accurately and fast enough to avoid a backlog. Search-based decoders such as Tesseract achieve high accuracy by finding a minimum-weight set of error events with an A* search, but their search effort grows rapidly with the physical error rate and the code size. To reduce this search effort while maintaining a logical error rate close to that of Tesseract, we propose a belief propagation (BP)-guided modification of the Tesseract decoder for quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Damped sum-product BP is applied to the triggered detectors before the Tesseract search. If the detectors triggered by the BP hard decision match the triggered detectors, this hard decision is accepted directly, and the Tesseract search is skipped. Otherwise, the BP marginal probability estimates, weighted by a trust coefficient, modify the search priority, while the path cost keeps the channel-prior weights so that the decoding objective is unchanged. The framework also supports BP-based initialization, in which selected BP decisions form the starting point of a residual search whose signed-cost objective allows incorrect initial decisions to be removed. A node-exploration limit bounds this residual search; if the limit is reached, the decoder falls back to the BP-guided search on the original triggered detector set. The method is evaluated on the [[72,12,6]], [[90,8,10]], and [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle codes under circuit-level noise. With BP-based initialization and a global trust coefficient, the number of Tesseract search nodes expanded is reduced by up to more than two orders of magnitude at low physical error rates, while the logical error rate remains close to that of Tesseract.

titles.title: Belief Propagation-Informed Tesseract Decoding of Quantum LDPC Codes

abstracts.value: Most quantum circuit platforms focus on idealized circuit assembly and simulation, hiding hardware compilation, error identification, and variational model training behind black-box operations. QYANTRAM addresses this gap through an open platform comprising four subsystems, built around evidence-backed results and independent verification. Its staged compilation pipeline makes every transformation traceable, while the router publishes rejected SWAP candidates and their scores for transparent decision-making. Verification exploits inactive qubits remaining in the |0> state, reducing complexity from 2^N to 2^k for k active qubits. This mathematically exact reduction enables full pre-compilation verification on 127- and 156-qubit layouts, achieving approximately 10,000x speed-ups with execution times below one millisecond. The error identification engine exhaustively evaluates all Pauli error patterns without sampling, matching closed-form predictions within 2.8e-17. Its machine-learning engine achieves numerical agreement within 2.0e-15 of qiskit.quantum_info while training 25-50 times faster. The router introduces approximately 1.27x more SWAP gates than Qiskit's SABRE due to its omission of optimization, trading routing efficiency for complete decision transparency and traceability.

titles.title: Qyantram: A Transparent and Verifiable Quantum Computing Platform

abstracts.value: We study hashing against quantum adversaries, as used in cryptographic applications, and provide bounds on the probability of failure in practical settings where seeds might be reused and might be non-ideal. Randomness extraction and privacy amplification are key components of quantum cryptographic protocols, such as quantum randomness generation or key distribution, that allow the compression of partially secure raw data into shorter output with high security. To ensure the security of any cryptographic construction that integrates them, it is desirable to establish composable security. This can be done by using methods based on universal hashing and leveraging the general leftover hash lemma, which allows extraction of near-uniform random numbers from an imperfect entropy source by sampling from an almost two-universal family of hash functions using a seed. This approach is taken in many practical implementations, commonly using Toeplitz hashing. The lemma provides an upper bound $\varepsilon$ on the distance of the output to uniform randomness, which holds on average over the choice of seeds. It makes no claim that any particular seed yields near-uniform random numbers. This poses a problem for practical applications where a seed is sampled once and reused for many rounds (blockwise hashing). Here, we study the subset of \textit{bad} seeds yielding far-from-uniform outputs. We show that randomness extraction against quantum side information is guaranteed to produce $δ$-close-to-uniform random numbers except with failure probability $\left(\frac{\varepsilon}δ\right)^2$. This result is generalised to blockwise hashing providing a guarantee of the security of $k$ rounds except with failure probability $\big(\frac{(2k-1)\varepsilon}δ\big)^2$. Moreover, we extend the general leftover hash lemma to blockwise hashing and relax the assumption of almost two-universality.

titles.title: On the Failure Probability of Quantum Leftover Hashing with Bad Seeds

abstracts.value: We consider the problem of graph private information retrieval (PIR) in the quantum setting. We focus on a specific type of graphs, namely the forest graphs. A forest graph is a union of disjoint trees. We consider the quantum setting where all the servers share an entangled state. Each server is allowed to send only one qudit per retrieval round. We design a scheme for the forest graphs that achieves the rate of $\frac{3}{N}$. The scheme uses a GHZ state as the initial entangled state between the servers prior to the scheme initiation. We compare our scheme with the only work done in the literature that considered the quantum setting of graph PIR. We show that our scheme is more efficient in this setting. We derive the quantum capacity for the case of $G=3K_2$, which is equal to $4/6$. $G=3K_2$ is a special case of the forest graph. We design a scheme that is specialized for this graph, achieving a rate equal to $4/6$ and provide the corresponding matching upper bound, establishing it as the capacity.

titles.title: Quantum Private Information Retrieval on Forests

abstracts.value: Quantum channel tomography (also known as quantum process tomography) is a fundamental task in quantum information and quantum computing, aiming to learn the full description of an unknown quantum channel from black-box queries. For channels with input dimension $d_1$, output dimension $d_2$, and Kraus rank at most $r$, [CGO+26] identifies the dilation rate $τ=rd_2/d_1\geq 1$ as a key parameter governing a Heisenberg-to-classical transition in query complexity. While the optimal bounds in the boundary regime ($τ=1$) and the away-from-boundary regime ($τ\geq 1+Ω(1)$) are now known, the precise behavior in the near-boundary regime ($1<τ<1+o(1)$) has remained unresolved. In this paper, we close this gap, thereby fully settling the query complexity of quantum channel tomography. Specifically, we show that the query complexity is - $Ω(rd_1d_2/\varepsilon^2)$ for diamond norm error $\varepsilon$, matching the upper bound by [MB26, CGO+26], - $Θ(d_1^2/\varepsilon+\min\{(τ-1)d_1^2,(τ-1)^2d_1^2d_2^2\}/\varepsilon^2)$ for Choi trace norm error $\varepsilon$. Our results reveal two qualitatively different forms of the Heisenberg-to-classical transition. For diamond norm tomography, the Heisenberg scaling disappears suddenly as soon as $τ$ leaves the boundary regime. In contrast, Choi trace norm tomography exhibits a gradual transition from Heisenberg to classical scaling as $τ$ moves from the boundary regime to the away-from-boundary regime.

titles.title: Quantum channel tomography: optimal bounds in the near-boundary regime

abstracts.value: We show that the causal structure of spacetime can emerge within the memory of a learning agent performing a quantum information task. We train a model-based reinforcement-learning agent to maximize the quantum mutual information between localized quantum probes interacting with a quantum field in Minkowski spacetime, without directly providing it with information regarding the spacetime metric or causal structure. In learning to accomplish this task, the reinforcement-learning agent constructs an internal predictive model whose planner develops the characteristic null structure of spacetime, allowing us to reconstruct the causal structure of the Minkowski metric with high accuracy. Within this task, spacetime geometry is obtained from an agent's successful predictions and actions, providing a first step toward showing that spacetime concepts emerge from operational quantum experience.

titles.title: Spacetime Emergence in the Memory of a Learning Agent

abstracts.value: Mapping the three-dimensional distribution of dark matter is key to tracing the growth of cosmic structure. Two-dimensional weak lensing mass maps recover its projected distribution, but they blend structures at different distances along the line of sight. We reconstruct the three-dimensional matter distribution in the 0.54 deg$^2$ COSMOS-Web field using deep James Webb Space Telescope imaging, with an effective source density of 121 galaxies arcmin$^{-2}$ We combine a physical weak lensing forward model with a diffusion-based Bayesian generative prior learned from cosmological simulations, yielding a posterior distribution of the matter field across 20 lens planes to $z \simeq 2$, doubling the redshift reach of previous Hubble Space Telescope-based 3D reconstructions and approaching cosmic noon, an epoch of rapid galaxy growth. The reconstruction separates structures that overlap in projection and recovers non-Gaussian matter structure across a range of spatial scales, including over-densities associated with independently identified galaxy clusters that were not detected in earlier weak lensing maps. Posterior sampling quantifies the range of three-dimensional matter distributions allowed by the data, enabling a probabilistic visualization of the cosmic web while propagating uncertainties in its inferred structure. Null and simulation-based tests show that the recovered structures are supported by the lensing signal and are consistent with expectations from the fiducial $Λ$CDM cosmology. These results extend three-dimensional weak lensing mapping into the high-redshift, non-Gaussian regime and establish a route towards probabilistic mapping of the evolving cosmic web with current wide-field lensing surveys.

titles.title: 3D dark matter map of the JWST COSMOS-Web field using diffusion-based generative priors

abstracts.value: We present a preconditioning pipeline that accelerates Tensor Train (TT) linear solvers for symmetric positive-definite problems. Extending the Factorized Sparse Approximate Inverse framework to tensor networks, we construct a preconditioner as the product of a TT operator and its transpose. This formulation is positive semidefinite for any bond dimension and truncation, and definite whenever the factor is non-singular, satisfying the mathematical requirements of the Conjugate Gradient method. We detail the construction of this preconditioner and its integration into Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG)-like linear solvers. Performance evaluations show consistent iteration reductions for anisotropic diffusion and Poisson problems across various configurations, leading to net speedups of up to 25% in ill-conditioned settings of time stepping schemes that can reuse the approximate inverses. These benchmarks were performed with the open-source Julia library DifferenTT.jl, which we also introduce in this work to provide out-of-the-box access to these preconditioned pipelines.

titles.title: Factorized approximate inverse preconditioners in the tensor train format

abstracts.value: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) processes temporal information through quantum dynamics, but it remains unclear whether small QRC models can forecast real data competitively with classical models and whether their predictions survive the transfer from ideal simulation to noisy hardware. We address both questions for a six-qubit gate-based reservoir that forecasts next-day motor-insurance claim counts. Five reservoir candidates were selected and frozen using hardware-native interaction graphs, Trotterized Ising dynamics, memory and measurement-robustness criteria, circuit cost, and calibrated-noise screening. On 232 held-out test days, the ideal candidates reached root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 5.66-6.12 claims/day, compared with 5.36 for ridge regression. For four of the five, the difference from ridge was not significant under a 95% block bootstrap, and their accuracy was comparable with classical recurrent and reservoir baselines. On the 156-qubit IBM Kingston processor, we ran 63 evaluations in 21 paired rounds, comparing hardware-aware, random-native, and Qiskit optimization level 1 layouts. Hardware-aware placement gave lower RMSE than Qiskit in every round, with a maximum transfer distortion of 7.59 claims/day (11.84 for Qiskit), and avoided the severe transfer failures seen for some random layouts. Most of the hardware distortion appeared as a systematic forecast shift, which a short hardware probe on training inputs detected before the test runs. Longer replay windows raised circuit cost without a consistent gain in forecasting accuracy or hardware transfer. Small QRC models can thus reach competitive accuracy on this task, and hardware-aware layout selection makes their transfer to IBM Kingston more consistent.

titles.title: Hardware-Aware Design and Layout Selection in Quantum Reservoir Computing for Insurance Claims Forecasting

abstracts.value: We construct $p$-adic polynomial approximations to the zero-framing cohomological quasimap vertex of cotangent bundles to complete flag varieties from the trigonometric Calogero--Moser system. Negative integer couplings give regular staircase Jack polynomials with nonnegative integer coefficients. We compare them with complete-flag master polynomials extending the construction of Smirnov--Varchenko. Both families converge coefficientwise to the vertex and satisfy the full commuting equations modulo $p^s$. For $n\geq3$, we prove sharp degree-dependent congruences and compute leading residues at every $p$-power scale. Their discrepancy has coefficient norm $p^{-1}$ and an exact weighted Gauss norm giving uniform decay on smaller closed polydiscs. For the master family, multivariable Dwork congruences reconstruct the vertex by an infinite product. The results hold in every rank for $0<r/d\leq1/2$ and odd prime $p$.

titles.title: Calogero-Moser Polynomial Approximations and Dwork Congruences for Complete Flags

abstracts.value: In the self-dual limit of Yang-Mills theory on Euclidean AdS$_4$ studied by Heuveline, Ruzziconi, Sheta and Strominger, the boundary condition of the second-order action becomes vacuous, but the boundary equation of the first-order action is non-trivial. We show that, with this equation, the vacuum is the only saddle with a real gauge field when both fields are smooth up to the conformal boundary, for any compact gauge group. In particular, the self-dual solutions of Sarioglu and Tekin (2009) are not saddles; we also correct their charges, which omitted a surface term at the conformal boundary. Complex saddles and singular limits remain open.

titles.title: No smooth real instanton saddles in self-dual Yang-Mills on AdS$_4$

abstracts.value: Recently, Pardon introduced a universal curve counting framework, which allows him to show that curve counting on 3-folds is "generated" by local curves (in a precise sense). We implement this universal curve counting program for Calabi-Yau 4-folds, where a significant technical difficulty comes from the dependence of the virtual dimension on the genus, which leads to more complicated generators than just local curves. Our main techniques are combinations of deformation-theoretic and homotopy-theoretic methods with an adaptation of Pardon's generic transversality results, which allow us to establish a full set of (computable) generators for CY4 curve counting. As a result, we prove (a slight correction of) the Gromov-Witten/Pandharipande-Thomas correspondence with primary descendents for CY4-folds, formulated by Cao, Maulik, and Toda. From this, we additionally obtain integrality of Gopakumar-Vafa style invariants for CY4-folds, as conjectured by Klemm-Pandharipande.

titles.title: Universal Curve Counting in Calabi-Yau 4-folds

abstracts.value: We construct an explicit small model for the $\infty$-groupoid of null-concordances of higher gauge curvatures by algorithmically trivializing their nonlinear Bianchi identities. More precisely, for a finite-type Sullivan minimal Bianchi algebra equipped with positive integer weights, we organize weighted potentials and higher gauge parameters at each fixed curvature into an $\infty$-groupoid whose gauge transformations are linear in the parameters. We prove that this model is naturally equivalent to the $\infty$-groupoid of null-concordances through an intermediate total-form model, with explicit projection and section maps and simplicial homotopies. When nonempty, its connected components form a torsor for the degree-zero cohomology of an associated weighted gauge complex, and its higher homotopy groups are computed by the higher cohomology of this complex.

abstracts.value: Symmetry-enforced gaplessness is a phenomenon in which a quantum system is forced to be gapless due to its global symmetry. Previous works have mainly focused on anomalous symmetries. Another approach, using symmetry spans, which specify two embeddings of a common symmetry into two larger symmetries, was proposed by the authors. In this work, we show that a symmetry span can enforce gaplessness even when both larger symmetries are invertible and non-anomalous: each alone admits a trivially gapped phase, but because the embeddings differ by a twist associated with a symmetry-protected topological phase, the symmetry they generate admits no gapped phase with finitely many ground states. We present such a span of a finite group and $\mathrm{U}(1)^2$ in 1+1 dimensions, with continuum realizations and a lattice Hamiltonian, with a finite-dimensional local Hilbert space and finitely many parameters, that is gapless in any region of its parameter space. We also discuss a 2+1-dimensional example and spans of only finite symmetries.

titles.title: Enforced Gaplessness by Combining Non-Anomalous Symmetries

abstracts.value: In this work we show that standard results in quantum tomography, which are typically proven in the context of Hilbert spaces, can analogously be established in the theory of Schwartz spaces. In particular, we will see that quantum states are equivalently characterized by their Wigner function, the characteristic of their Wigner function, and the probability distributions for a family of linear combinations of position and momentum. Physically, the latter can be understood as the evolution of its probability distribution in position over time under, for example, free or harmonic evolution. The result is obtained with techniques that are more accessible to a physicist audience, and shows that, at least for tomography results, the full structure of Hilbert spaces is not necessary.

titles.title: Quantum tomography on Schwartz space

abstracts.value: We prove propagation estimates for extensive fermionic many-body interactions with polynomial time growth, no loss of spatial decay, and an optimal threshold for the polynomial spatial exponent. More precisely, we construct local representatives of evolved fermionic many-body interactions on metric spaces with polynomial volume growth of order $d_{\mathrm{vol}}$ and suitable cell partitions. For the even Hamiltonian interaction $Φ_u$ and the even interaction $Ψ$ being evolved, we assume bounds, uniform in the site, on sums of term norms over finite supports $X$ containing a given site, with weights $e^{κ|X|}(1+\operatorname{diam}X)^a$ and $e^{κ|X|}(1+\operatorname{diam}X)^p$, respectively. Here $a>d_{\mathrm{vol}}$, $0\le p\le a$, $κ$ is sufficiently large, and the Hamiltonian bound is uniform in time. We construct local representatives whose interaction norms with weight $e^{c(1+|t-s|)^{-b}|X|}(1+\operatorname{diam}X)^p$ grow at most polynomially in $|t-s|$, for suitable $c,b>0$. In particular, $p=a$ is allowed: the Hamiltonian need not decay faster than the interaction being evolved. The threshold $a>d_{\mathrm{vol}}$ is optimal in general: uniform polynomial time bounds at $p=a$ fail for $0<a\le d_{\mathrm{vol}}$, even for smooth time-dependent two-site interactions. Polynomial time growth permits integration against filters with sufficiently many finite absolute moments, including those used in quasi-adiabatic constructions and quantum belief propagation. We derive consequences for filtered interactions and the dynamics they generate, providing dynamical estimates for perturbation theory with extensive perturbations, including gap stability, the principle that local perturbations perturb locally (LPPL), adiabatic theory, and response theory. All results also hold for quantum spin systems.

titles.title: Lossless propagation bounds for long-range fermionic interactions

abstracts.value: We develop a numerical conformal bootstrap for two-dimensional CFTs with $c>1$ based on Virasoro conformal blocks, computed with Zamolodchikov's recursion and optimal polynomial interpolation. As a first test we isolate an island around three decoupled Ising models. We then consider three 3-state Potts models coupled through their energy operators, a candidate irrational CFT. Mixed correlators isolate the decoupled theory in an island, and different gap assumptions, motivated by perturbation theory, yield a peninsula that contains the coupled fixed point but not the decoupled one. Finally, we explore the standard single-correlator bound on the lowest-dimension scalar primary in the OPE of two identical scalars. We find that for central charges just above $c=1$ the bound collapses over a wide range of external dimensions. This excludes any theory whose lightest scalar is absent from its own OPE and lies in this range, and supports the conjecture that no compact CFT exists in this region. We explain several features of these bounds analytically.

titles.title: The Virasoro Bootstrap: from the $c\sim1$ desert to coupled Potts

abstracts.value:
We show that the vacuum partition function of the $q$-deformed oscillator 
\[ L_q(z):= \langle0|e^{zT_q}|0\rangle, \qquad T_q := \mathsf{a}_q + \mathsf{a}_q^* \]
 satisfies the Lee-Yang property, i.e., all zeros of $L_q$ lie on the imaginary line for all $q\in[-1, 1)$, proving the conjectures of Okuyama'23. Using the connection between $q$-deformed oscillators and the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) Hamiltonian in the doubly-scaled regime, we show that the annealed SYK partition function satisfies the Lee-Yang property in the thermodynamic limit, that is, all of its Fisher zeros are on the imaginary axis. As a result, we show that the quenched SYK partition function admits a zero-free strip of constant width with high probability, rigorously complementing the large$-k$ replica calculations of Zlokapa and Kiani'26. We show the imaginary-rootedness of $L_q$ by expressing $φ_q(z):= L_q(\mathbf{i} z)$ as a locally uniform limit of ``$q$-deformed'' matching polynomials and then showing that those $q$-deformed polynomials are real-rooted. This establishes that $φ_q$ is real-rooted, and in fact belongs to the \emph{Laguerre-Pólya} class. The real-rootedness of the $q$-deformed polynomials yields novel log-concavity relations on the \emph{$q$-deformed matching moments}
\[M_\ell(q):= \sum_{π\in\mathcal{P}_2(2\ell)}q^{\operatorname{cr}(π)}.\]
 We show the real-rootedness of the $q$-deformed polynomials by using the Touchard--Riordan formula to derive a partial differential equation relating their $q$-derivatives to their $z$-derivatives, and then analyzing the resulting motion of their roots.

abstracts.value: The ensemble average of Narain conformal field theories over their moduli space is a real-analytic Eisenstein series, whose Poincaré expansion can be interpreted as a sum over lens spaces weighted by the partition functions of Abelian Chern-Simons theory. In this paper we extend this correspondence from lens spaces to Seifert manifolds, which gives an example of a restricted sum over topologies of the kind that arises in three-dimensional quantum gravity. A Seifert manifold is obtained from a fixed core, a punctured surface times a circle, by gluing solid tori to its boundary tori, and we place a copy of the Narain theory on each of these tori. The ensemble average supplies the sum over the solid tori, or more precisely over marked presentations with fixed base genus, number of fibers and integer Seifert invariant. The resulting sum converges absolutely and is a polynomial in the components of the vector-valued Eisenstein series. When all the boundary tori share a single modulus, the average acquires connected corrections, which we identify with wormholes gluing the core to itself; for two boundary tori, the terms with rational Lagrangian sublattices of the Siegel-Eisenstein series are realized by wormholes containing an exceptional fiber. After reduction along the fiber, the construction closely parallels the two-dimensional topological gravity of Marolf and Maxfield, with the base of the fibration playing the role of their spacetime. We also discuss Dehn fillings of 3-manifolds with torus boundary, non-orientable bases, and the surgery formula. Our results suggest that modularity could be an organizing principle in the summation of geometries in quantum gravity.

titles.title: Summing over Seifert Manifolds in Narain Ensemble Averages

abstracts.value: We show that the Belinski-Zakharov soliton construction factorizes into signed Pfaffian tau-functions, revealing a pure-spinor description of the metric and its regularity conditions. We derive analytic restrictions on the integral rod data, prove uniqueness for the asymptotically flat balance problem at fixed rod structure and periods, and give a conditional criterion for global existence. Combining these results with exhaustive enumeration of the admissible data and rigorous existence certificates, we construct a catalogue of regular asymptotically flat solutions representing 356 rod-word classes through twelve turning points, and 52 isolated regular asymptotically locally flat solutions through eight turning points. Analytic positivity and smooth-completion results establish regularity beyond the finite numerical solve. Based on this catalogue, we investigate two organizations of the solution space: generalized rank-two root systems and compositions of simpler endpoint geometries. The endpoint composition rules reproduce exactly all retained asymptotically flat words through twelve turning points.

abstracts.value: The algebraic and environmental characteristics of mixed unitary quantum operations are investigated. abstracts.value: Nuclear structure is closely connected to anisotropic flow in central heavy-ion collisions (HICs), so flow observables provide important probes for constraining nuclear deformation. Conventional Monte Carlo (MC) models typically describe deformed nuclei as classical rotors with definite orientations, whereas the ground states of even--even nuclei with $J=0$ are rotationally invariant. Motivated by the importance of rotational symmetry restoration, we systematically investigate symmetric collisions involving the representative even--even nuclei $^{20}\mathrm{Ne}$, $^{28}\mathrm{Si}$, $^{96}\mathrm{Ru}$, and $^{238}\mathrm{U}$ using an extended MC Glauber model that incorporates quantum superposition of nuclear orientations. In the final state, the quantum treatment suppresses elliptic flow $v_2\{2\}$, with the strongest effect observed in ultra-central Ne+Ne collisions. Quantum superposition further induces system-dependent changes in normalized symmetric cumulants and shifts the Pearson correlation between $v_2^2$ and $[p_T]$ toward the corresponding near-spherical reference values. Moreover, the quantum treatment modifies cross-system flow ratios and the U+U/Au+Au covariance ratio used experimentally to constrain nuclear deformation parameters. Our results suggest that the quantum-rotor treatment may affect the interpretation of nuclear structure information inffered from heavy-ion collision final-state observables.
